findings.title: Burst-regression cause given as the watcher's preemption, which the results say was never measured
findings.scenario: CLAUDE.md:2226-2228 says "the watcher's preemption lengthens gaps inside a burst", and cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:38 repeats it as fact. The data does not support this. v3/README.md item 1 (line 77-78) and v3/review/review.json (c05 entry, caveat c) say: "What creates the mid-burst gaps of 50 us or more (presumably the watcher's preemption) is not measured." They also name the path that was measured: AC2 and AC4 skipped their deferral sleeps 4,000-4,600 times per run (AC3 350-440) through the late-sleep guard and fell into 100 us sleeps. Without load (c06, no guard skips) the same rules cost only 0.4-0.5 us more per call. A maintainer who trusts the comment could try to cut preemption (priority, affinity) or keep the two-gap rule for that reason, and miss the guard/slow-sleep interaction the counters actually show.
findings.fix: Say it is presumed and not measured ("presumably the watcher's preemption; not measured"), and state the measured path: under load the closed window plus late-guard skips sent the watcher into 100 us sleeps (guard_skips 4,000-4,600 vs 350-440). Change both CLAUDE.md:2227 and cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:38.

findings.title: Dense-request trade-off credits AC2's polling to closing on one long gap; its 2x-gap window sizing is the cause
findings.scenario: CLAUDE.md:2224 reads: "a window closed by one long gap kept polling there, 47.5-52.8 us, for 30-37 us more CPU per launch". The numbers are AC2's (v3 c31, per-round per-launch mean 51.5/47.5/52.8/52.7). But AC4 also reacts to a single gap of 50 us or more (it halves the window), and in c31 it sleeps like AC3: 57.4 us per launch, 35.3-39.5 us CPU per launch, win80=0. v3 README item 4 groups it with AC3 and ACn as the sets that sleep. What sets AC2 apart in c31 is its max(2 x gap, 10) sizing: win80=24840 of 30001 requests, against AC3's win20 17615 and win0 12386. A reader would conclude that reacting to a single long gap buys dense-request throughput. The data shows it was the gap-based sizing.
findings.fix: Name the rule that polled: "a window sized 2x the last gap (v2's AC2) kept polling there". Optionally note that AC4, which halves on one long gap, did not.

findings.title: 20.7 us and the 32% lower bound belong to AC4, which halves the window rather than closing it
findings.scenario: CLAUDE.md:2226-2227 reads: "A window closed by one long gap made 32-call bursts under full load cost 20.7-22.1 us per call". 22.1 is AC2 (closes on one gap). 20.7 is AC4, which halves the window on each long gap and closes only below 10 us (v3 README set table; c05 AC4 per round 22.08/20.72/20.70/20.76). The policy header says it correctly: "One long gap closing it (or halving it)". The test comment at runtime/unit-test/test_cuda_watcher_policy.cpp:11 has the same misattribution: "closing it on one gap of 50 us or more made 32-call bursts ... 32-41% dearer". 41% = AC2/AC3 (22.1/15.7), but 32% = AC4/AC3 (20.7/15.7), the halving set. v2's AC2/AC (22.1/16.9 = 31%) falls outside the quoted range, although the comment cites "v2 and v3". A reader takes the whole range as the cost of closing on one gap.
findings.fix: Write "A window closed (AC2: 22.1) or halved (AC4: 20.7) by one long gap ..." in CLAUDE.md, and "closing or halving it on one gap" in test_cuda_watcher_policy.cpp:11.

findings.title: "Measured ... (448 runs, 4 rounds)" also covers figures from other rounds; the AC3 latch was not tested in v3
findings.scenario: CLAUDE.md:2215 opens with "Measured against the earlier policies (448 runs, 4 rounds):" and then gives "idle 0.002 of a core parked (0.011 sleeping 100 us at a time)" (line 2221). That is cell c11, which is not among v3's 14 cells and was never run with AC3. The figures come from the main round (504 runs: AC 0.002, M100 0.011) and v2 (304 runs: AC/AC2 0.002). The latch paragraph's "graph launches 69-70 us per call, WFE without the latch 533 us" (line 2242) likewise comes from main and v2 c18 (A/AC/AC2 and W). v3/README.md says no v3 run latched and that "graph launches with the v3 rules" were not tested ("The latch rule shared by AC2-ACn was tested in v2 only"). The CLAUDE.md "Not tested" list (line 2229) leaves this out, along with the 50-65 us gap edge. A reader takes the idle and graph numbers as measured for the committed AC3 policy in the cited 448-run set.
findings.fix: Cite the source of each borrowed figure, e.g. "idle (c11, main round and v2, sets AC/AC2): 0.002 vs 0.011" and "graph launches (v2 c18, AC2's latch): 69-70 us". Add "graph launches and the latch with these window rules, the 50-65 us edge" to the Not-tested list.

findings.title: Cause of isolated latch hits stated as established; v2 calls it the likely mechanism
findings.scenario: CLAUDE.md:2244-2247 says isolated hits come from a process's first probed launch, "whose note follows the first-time lookup in note_launch_if_probed and arrives after its kernel posted". cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:115-116 says the same in short. v2/README.md item 5 supports only the first part: 4 of 4 isolated hits had h0_note=0. It gives the lookup-delay explanation as "Likely mechanism", backed by one run's h0_any=1. controls/README.md item 6 also had an isolated hit (c02 AC0, 2-3 ms kernels, no load) that the earlier assumed cause did not explain. Nothing timed the first-time lookup against the kernel's first post. A reader would treat the cause as proven and could rule out other sources of spurious hits, which matter because two of them within 1 s latch the watcher out of parking.
findings.fix: Keep the observation ("isolated hits came at a process's first probed launch: no note seen yet, 4 of 4 in v2") and mark the mechanism as likely or not timed, in both CLAUDE.md and cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:115.

result.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The data supports the finding.

What the dev change says:
- CLAUDE.md:2226-2228 (diff line 80): "A window closed by one long gap made 32-call bursts under full load cost 20.7-22.1 us per call: the watcher's preemption lengthens gaps inside a burst".
- runtime/src/attach/cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:36-38 (diff line 796): "...made 32-call bursts under full CPU load cost 20.7-22.1 instead of 15.7 us per call: the watcher's own preemption lengthens gaps inside a burst."
- Neither qualifies the claim. Both present it as the cause.

What the results say:
- The 20.7-22.1 us number is measured and correct (v3 table: AC2 22.1, AC4 20.7, AC3 15.7).
- The cause is not measured, and the results say so in every place they discuss it:
  - /home/jetson/src/results/gpu/watcher-policy-20261112/v3/README.md lines 77-78: "What creates the mid-burst gaps of 50 us or more (presumably the watcher's preemption) is not measured."
  - v3/review/review.json, c05 claim, caveat (c): "What creates the mid-burst gaps of 50 us or more (presumably watcher preemption) was not measured."
  - The same file, claim 8 (c): "Why AC2/AC3 stop polling under load was not isolated." It names other plausible causes: real host-thread delays, and the late guard sending the watcher straight to 100 us slow sleeps.
  - v2/README.md item 3: "inferred from the counters, not tested."
- The path the counters do show runs through the late-sleep guard (v3 README item 1 and review caveat (b)):
  - Under load, AC2/AC4 logged about 3,962-4,631 guard_skips per run, against 351-442 for AC3/AC5 and 607-659 for AC. The skipped deferral sleeps were followed by 100 us slow sleeps.
  - In c06 (no load, 0 guard skips), the same rules cost only 0.4-0.5 us more per call.
- The only source that states the preemption mechanism as fact is the working note v3/scripts/CLAIMS-v3.md claim 8. The review marked that claim "partly": "an interpretation that the logs do not test directly" and "untested and partly contradicted". The README corrected it to "presumably ... not measured".

Conclusion: the CLAUDE.md text and the header comment turn a hypothesis the results flag as unmeasured into a fact. They also leave out the guard-skip path, which is the one the counters measured.

Impact: this is documentation only and does not change runtime behaviour, so medium severity may be high. The scenario is still concrete. The comment sits right on top of poll_window's two-gap rule and gives the reason for it. Someone tuning this code could chase scheduler priority or affinity for the watcher, or reason about the close rule, and overlook the late-guard to 100 us slow-sleep interaction that the data shows.

Fix as the finding proposes: mark the cause as presumed and unmeasured, and state the measured guard_skips path. Make the change in both CLAUDE.md:2227 and cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:38.

The finding is correct. It is a low-severity documentation error and does not affect the code.

Evidence:
- **AC2 and AC4 rules:** In the v3 README set table, AC2 closes its window on one gap of 50 us or more. AC4 instead halves the window on each such gap and closes it only below 10 us. The experimental code agrees (/home/jetson/src/bpftime-gpu-work/policy/src/runtime/src/attach/bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:399-407, WMODE == 4: `win /= 2; if (win < WIN_START) win = 0`).
- **c05 numbers:** In v3/summary.md, c05 cost per call is AC2 22.1, AC4 20.7, AC3 15.7. The per-round values in v3/review/review.json are AC2 22.15/22.12/21.53/22.64 and AC4 22.08/20.72/20.70/20.76. So the low end, 20.7, is AC4's median. The rule that closes on one gap (AC2) never went below 21.5 in any round.
- **CLAUDE.md:2226-2227:** It says "A window closed by one long gap made 32-call bursts under full load cost 20.7-22.1 us per call". That range mixes the halving set (AC4) into the closing set (AC2). The new header (cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:36-37) words the same claim correctly: "One long gap closing it (or halving it)".
- **test_cuda_watcher_policy.cpp:10-12:** It says "closing it on one gap ... 32-41% dearer". 22.1/15.7 is +41% (AC2), but 20.7/15.7 is +32% (AC4, the halving set). Measured against AC3, AC2 alone would be +37-47% per round. The v2 contrast the comment also cites is 22.1/16.9, +31%, which falls outside the stated range.
- **Both lines are new in this change:** dev.diff lines 80 and 926.

The conclusion behind the policy still holds: reacting to a single long gap is what hurts, and AC3 needs two long gaps in a row. Only the attribution of the 20.7 us / 32% figures is wrong, so this is a factual error rather than a style point. Fix: say "closed (AC2: 22.1) or halved (AC4: 20.7)" in CLAUDE.md, and "closing or halving it on one gap" in the test comment.

This is a real misattribution, though low severity (docs only, no code effect).

The strongest refutation would be that "a window closed by one long gap" at /home/jetson/src/bpftime-daily-state/worktrees/4708f4092d1e/candidate/CLAUDE.md:2224 only names AC2 and claims no cause. The next sentence (line 2226) rules that out. It uses the same phrase for "32-call bursts under full load cost 20.7-22.1 us per call". In the c05 row of /home/jetson/src/results/gpu/watcher-policy-20261112/v3/README.md, 20.7 is AC4's figure and 22.1 is AC2's, so in the doc the label covers both AC2 and AC4.

Applied the same way to the dense-request cell c31, the line-2224 claim ("kept polling there, 47.5-52.8 us, for 30-37 us more CPU per launch") does not hold for AC4. In /home/jetson/src/results/gpu/watcher-policy-20261112/v3/summary.md, AC4 in c31 has:
- a per-launch mean of 57.4 us,
- 35.3-39.5 us of CPU per launch,
- win80=0 (win0=18017, win20=11984),
- about 0.93M hot iterations, against 10.4M for AC2.

AC3 and AC4 differ only in how they react to a single gap of 50 us or more, which v3 README item 1 calls a controlled contrast. Both sleep in c31, so reacting to one long gap is not what made AC2 poll. AC5 shows the same thing from the other side: it uses AC3's close rule yet polls (win80=29994, about 13M hot iterations), so polling in c31 does not follow the close rule in either direction.

The finding overreaches in one place: no tested set changes only the window sizing, since AC2 and AC4 differ in both sizing and close-versus-halve. Still, the counters and the code point to the sizing. AC2's window sat in the 21-80 us bucket for 24840 of 30001 requests, while AC3 and AC4 never left win0/win20. In run_policy_watcher (/home/jetson/src/bpftime-gpu-work/policy/src/runtime/src/attach/bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp), the V2 mode-2 branch sets win = min(max(2*gap,10),50) in one step, so a single missed gap of 25-49 us opens a 50 us window that then catches every request. Modes 3 and 4 only double on a missed short gap and get closed or halved before reaching 40 us. Closing on one gap can only shrink the window. In fact AC2 closes less often in c31 than AC3 (win0 5161 against 12386), because its windows are large enough to catch the requests.

The 47.5-52.8 us and 30-37 us figures match v3 README item 4 (AC2 against AC3), so the numbers are right. The fault is the rule they are credited to. A reader of CLAUDE.md, which nowhere describes AC2's 2x-gap sizing, would conclude that closing on one long gap buys dense-request throughput. The data shows that rule sleeps like AC3, and the same doc says it costs bursts under load. The suggested wording, "a window sized 2x the last gap kept polling there", correctly names AC2.

findings.title: WFE opt-in: probed-kernel end now detected every 1 ms instead of every 100 us, so WFE holds the core up to ~1 ms after the last kernel
findings.scenario: BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1 on aarch64 with EVTSTRM. The old loop (46f5a7cb) called any_running() every 100 us while on the flag (cuda_watcher_kernel_check). The WFE block now calls kernels_may_run(), which re-queries the events only every event_query_every_us = 1000 us and resets that timer at every new note. Example: a probed 1 ms kernel launched every 2-3 ms. The old loop left WFE about 100 us after each kernel ended and parked or slept between launches. The new loop stays in WFE (counted as running, holding its core) for up to ~1 ms after each kernel, so for most of the idle time between launches. In the c09-style low-duty case (2 ms kernel, 18 ms idle) that is about +0.05 core over W's measured 0.156. The opt-in WFE numbers quoted in CLAUDE.md come from the old cadence, and this change is neither measured nor documented. The default AC3 path is unaffected: the experiment also used EVQ_EVERY=1000.
findings.fix: When wfe is set, query the events every 100 us (for example, a separate cadence constant passed into kernels_may_run on the WFE branch), keeping 1 ms for the sleeping path that AC3 measured. Or document and measure the 1 ms cadence for WFE mode.

findings.title: WFE opt-in: the unseen-launch latch now makes the watcher WFE-wait continuously, holding a core while no kernel runs
findings.scenario: BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1 with an application whose probed launches the hooks do not note: CUDA graphs, or a default nvcc 13 build launching through kernel handles (the v2 smoke test showed these latch every run). Example: a 1 ms probed kernel with one host call every 500 ms. Two backstop hits latch the watcher. Every later request is served while !inflight, which counts as evidence, so the latch never comes off. Because the WFE branch takes on_flag = kernels_may_run(t) = inflight || latched, the watcher sits in WFE the whole time: about one full core counted as running for the life of the process, although a kernel runs about 0.2% of the time. Previous dev never entered WFE for unnoted launches; it slept 50 us doubling to 1 ms, about 0.002-0.01 core, at 0-1 ms latency. Under full CPU load, measured W cost the load 13% of its throughput and 11% of host calls over 1 ms; that cost now also applies to idle periods of such apps. The CLAUDE.md contract says WFE holds its core while any probed kernel runs, not while latched and idle. This is not measured.
findings.fix: In the WFE branch, use WFE only for inflight (noted launches) and let the latched case take the 100 us slow sleeps as in the default path. Or explicitly document and measure WFE-while-latched.

result.reasoning:
This is a real error, but only in where the numbers came from. The values themselves are probably right for AC3, so the severity is low.

Checked in the data:
- **448 runs is v3 alone.** v3/verify.csv has 448 data rows, main has 504 and v2 has 304. v3/scripts/rounds-v3-cells.txt lists 14 cells: c31, c32, c23, c24, c21, c25-c28, c05, c06, c01, c02, c15. It has no c11 (idle agent) and no c18 (graphs).
- **The figures under that label.** The sentence opened by "Measured against the earlier policies (448 runs, 4 rounds)" at CLAUDE.md:2215 traces to v3 cells for everything but one:
  - c02 AC3: 69.3 / 108.3
  - c05: 15.7 / 16.9 / 16.6
  - c25: 45.2 / 43.2 / 54.4
  - c23: 0.104 / 1.039 / 1.028
  - c24: 0.26% / 2.74% / 2.80%
  - c31 and c21 as cited
  The exception is "idle 0.002 of a core parked (0.011 sleeping 100 us at a time)" at :2221. That is c11 from the main round (AC 0.002, M100 0.011) and v2 (AC/AC2 0.002), never run with AC3.
- **Graph figures.** The latch paragraph's "graph launches 69-70 us per call, WFE without the latch 533 us" (:2242) comes from c18 in the main round (AC 69.7, W 533.3) and v2 (AC 69.1, AC2 69.6).
- **v3 README.** It says the A part (park, latch) is not exercised in v3 ("no graph cells; no run latched"). It lists "the 50-65 us edge" and "graph launches with the v3 rules" as not tested, and says the latch was tested in v2 only.
- **CLAUDE.md "Not tested" list (:2229).** It names only alternating gaps and several processes.
- **No other source.** No AC3 run of an idle or graph cell exists elsewhere: v3/logs.tar.xz has no c11 or c18 entries, and ac3dev/ holds only build, mutation and regression logs. The rest of the section has no sentence giving the idle or graph figures their own rounds.
- **In scope.** dev.diff adds all of these lines (+ lines 68, 74, 95).

How strong each part is:
- **Idle figure: strongest, a factual misstatement.** It sits inside a sentence explicitly labelled with the v3 run set and is the only number there not in v3.
- **Graph figures: weaker.** They are in a separate paragraph without the 448 label. The misattribution is only by implication from "set AC3 of v3" and the missing "Not tested" entry.
- **Missing "Not tested" entries: on their own closer to a nit.** They matter mainly because the doc gives a graph number for the current rules.

Why the values are still likely correct for AC3:
- The park and latch code is v2's in every v3 set, and the dev latch matches v2's rule (two hits within 1 s, unlatch after 1 s).
- In c18 the window never engages (counters win0 = 100%, hot_iters = 0).
- In c02 (2-3 ms gaps) AC, AC2 and AC3 are indistinguishable (69.6 / 69.4 / 69.3).

So the failure is a reader looking for the idle number in the 448-run set and not finding it, or believing AC3 was measured with graphs. The policy itself does not behave differently.

Fix: name the source of each borrowed figure ("idle, c11 of the main round and v2: 0.002 vs 0.011"; "graphs, c18 of the main round and v2, the same latch rule: 69-70 us"). Add "graph launches and the latch with these window rules; the 50-65 us edge" to the Not-tested list.

The finding holds, and the data shows a bigger problem than the reviewer described: the measurements contradict the universal claim, not just the certainty of its wording.

Where the claim appears:
- CLAUDE.md:2244-2247: "Isolated hits come from a process's first probed launch, whose note follows the first-time lookup in `note_launch_if_probed` and arrives after its kernel posted."
- runtime/src/attach/cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:115-116 says the same thing in short.

1. The "first probed launch" part is false for the shipped rule.
- v3 used the same park/hit rule as dev: generation unchanged, a full 1 ms backstop, and flag1==1.
- I extracted v3/logs.tar.xz and searched the .stats files. There are 31 isolated hits and no run latched.
- 29 of them have h0_note=0, meaning no note had been seen yet.
- Two do not: v3 r4 c28_AC2 (h0_note=5127, h0_idle=2014) and v3 r4 c28_AC3 (h0_note=4250, h0_idle=2016). AC3 is wmode=3, the policy now in dev. c28 is 4 calls per launch under full load.
- In the experimental watcher, h0_note = t - t_gen_seen. t_gen_seen starts at 0 and is set only when the generation changes (policy bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:329/441/601). So these two hits came 4-5 ms after the watcher saw a note.
- They cannot be a first launch. The victim (v2/scripts/victim/spin3.cu, run by v3's run_one.sh) has one kernel function, spinKernel. Its first launch is a warm-up on the default stream before the timed loop, so the first-time lookup and the stream's first cuEventCreate both happen at warm-up.
- The cause of these two hits is not established by the data. A launcher delayed between original() and note() under load is possible, but nothing timed it.

2. The mechanism is not established either.
- For hits with no note seen, "the note arrives after its kernel posted" is nearly forced. The hooks call note_launch_if_probed only after original() returns (nv_attach_impl_frida_setup.cpp:206/553).
- Nothing shows the first-time lookup is the slow step. The doc's own evidence points elsewhere: h0_any=1 means any_running()'s try-lock failed, so the launcher was inside note() holding event_mutex. That is after the lookup had returned, around cuEventCreate/cuEventRecord.
- v2/README item 5 calls this the "Likely mechanism". The doc states it as fact. v3 has 6 more h0_note=0 hits with h0_any=1, which also place the delay inside note().

Impact is low but concrete. The doc tells readers that isolated hits happen only at start-up. A reader who sees the latch engage in a non-graph application under CPU load would wrongly conclude that unnoted launches (graphs, unresolved handles) are present. In fact non-start-up hits do occur under full load. Two of them within 1 s would latch the watcher out of parking into 100 us sleeps until 1 s with no unnoted requests. No measured run latched this way, so the latch is possible, not observed.

The reviewer's proposed fix ("4 of 4 in v2") would still overstate. The text should say that most isolated hits (29 of 31 in v3, 4 of 4 in v2) came before any note was seen, that 2 came under full load 4-5 ms after a note with the cause unknown, and that the lookup-delay mechanism is untimed. This applies to both CLAUDE.md and cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:115.

The mechanism holds, so this is real at low severity. Several of the finding's impact numbers are wrong and are corrected below.

Code facts:
- In the new loop (bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:363-373), the WFE branch decides whether to stay on the flag with kernels_may_run(t), lines 327-351. That function calls activity.any_running() only when t - last_event_query >= w::event_query_every_us, which is 1000 us (cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:28).
- It also sets last_event_query = t at every new generation (line 332).
- No other path clears `inflight` in WFE mode.
- The removed 46f5a7cb loop, still at git HEAD, checked any_running() every cuda_watcher_kernel_check = 100 us while on_flag was set, no matter how many notes arrived.
- Linux arm64's event stream (ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US = 100) ends each WFE within about 100 us, so the new loop sees a kernel's end only at the next 1 ms point after the note, plus up to about 100 us.
- When probed launches come less than 1 ms apart, every note resets the timer, so the events are never queried and the watcher stays in WFE (running, holding its core) for as long as the launches continue. The old loop dropped out of WFE between kernels.

Scenario: BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1 on the Orin, with a 100 us probed kernel launched every 800 us.
- Old loop: about 100-200 us of WFE, then 200 us of spinning, then a sleep until the next note. About 0.5 core.
- New loop: WFE for the whole period. About 1 core.

Corrections to the finding:
- The old loop did not "leave WFE about 100 us after each kernel ended and park". On leaving WFE it set last_request = now and spun on cpu_relax for the 200 us busy window. So the old loop also held the core for about 300 us after a kernel ended. The new path has no such spin.
- At c09-like low duty (rounds.sh: 2 ms spin, 18 ms gap), the extra WFE time per kernel is 0-1 ms depending on phase, roughly a few hundred us on average. The closest measured proxy is AB, which uses WFE behind the same EVQ_EVERY=1000 event query: 0.170 core against W's 0.156, so about +0.01-0.02 core, not +0.05.
- There is no latency or correctness effect. The WFE test only asks the watcher to leave the flag within 100 ms, so no test fails.

Why it still counts: no measured set has dev's exact opt-in WFE path.
- W is 46f5a7cb's own build (README line 40).
- The B sets used a load gate and a hot poll.
- The v2 and v3 READMEs contain no WFE sets.
- The CLAUDE.md costs quoted for WFE (13% throughput, 11% of calls over 1 ms) and the code comment at lines 198-207 come from the old 100 us cadence. The comment ("the event stream ends every wait within about 100 us too, so the watcher still sees its stop flag and a kernel's end") no longer holds for a kernel's end.

The default AC3 path is unaffected: the experiment also used EVQ_EVERY=1000 with the same reset on a new generation. Fix: query every 100 us on the WFE branch, or measure and document the 1 ms cadence for WFE mode.

Confirmed by tracing the candidate loop in runtime/src/attach/bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp together with cuda_watcher_policy.hpp. Severity is low.

How it happens:
1. Setup: BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1 on aarch64 with EVTSTRM. The application's probed kernels come from launches no hook notes, for example CUDA graphs. Each kernel makes one host call, every 500 ms.
2. Before the latch: activity.generation() never changes, so `inflight` stays false. `kernels_may_run` returns false, the WFE branch falls through, and the watcher parks with `wait_for_note(g0, 1ms)`.
3. Latching: a request still waiting when a park ends at its backstop is a hit (`latch.on_hit`). Two hits 500 ms apart are within `unseen_hit_window_us` (1 s), so the watcher latches.
4. Staying latched: from then on every request is served with `!inflight && generation()==seen_launches`. So `latch.on_request(t, true)` renews `last_evidence`, and `latched()` never passes `unlatch_after_us`.
5. Continuous WFE: `kernels_may_run` returns `inflight || latched`, which is now true. The WFE branch sets `on_flag=true` and calls `wait_while_equal(&comm->flag1, 0)`, then `continue`. Every WFE ends within about 100 us at the event stream, and the loop goes straight back into WFE. The thread never blocks, so the scheduler counts it as running about all the time, although the kernels run about 0.2% of the time.

Previous dev did not do this. The removed lines in dev.diff show that `on_flag` was set only when `activity.generation() != seen_launches`, i.e. for noted launches. Unnoted launches went to `wait_for_note(seen_launches, idle_sleep)`, 50 us doubling to 1 ms.

Why "it is opt-in, so intended" does not hold:
- The measured WFE-while-latched was gated. In the experiment's run_policy_watcher, a latched watcher reached `wfe_wait()` only through `B && gate_check(t)`, the load gate with its trip on late returns.
- The ungated W set used WFE on noted launches only. README finding 7 gives 533 us on graphs for it.
- So ungated WFE combined with the latch is new, and neither round measured it. v3/README says no v3 run latched, and the latch was tested in v2 only.
- The candidate's CLAUDE.md and the comment in the cpp state the WFE cost as holding the core "while any probed kernel runs". It is not stated for latched idle periods.

Scope and caveats:
- The hold lasts only while unnoted requests keep coming about once a second or more often. Sparser requests never latch. A burst leaves a 1 s WFE tail before the watcher parks again.
- "For the life of the process" is right for the 500 ms example, not in general.
- The 13% throughput and 11% over-1-ms figures are W under full CPU load with kernels actually running. Applying them to latched idle periods is an extrapolation. On an idle machine the cost is a thread counted as running.
- The precondition rests on graph launches. The claim that default nvcc 13 builds latch comes from the experiment build's smoke test, and the candidate docs hedge it ("when they are not resolved").

Fix options (either one):
- In the WFE branch, use WFE only while `inflight`, and let a latched watcher take the 100 us slow sleeps as the default path does.
- Or document the full-core hold while latched and measure it.

findings.title: Latch test's latency check cannot tell a latched watcher from one that still parks: phase-locked parked latency (~195 us) sits right at the 200 us threshold
findings.scenario: `bpftime_test_spaced_calls` (PTX lines 389-395) starts each 2 ms wait when the previous call returns, so every request comes at a fixed offset (about R+2005 us) from the end of the watcher's last service (R). A watcher that keeps parking after the latch does this after each request: 8 deferral sleeps of about 23.9 us each (v3 c02 AC3 stats: us_defer 612388 / 25608), then parks of about 1003 us each (us_park 295887 / 295). The second park ends near R+2197 us. Each call would therefore be answered in about 8*23.9 + 2*1003 - 2005 ≈ 195 us, every time. That figure is computed from those stats, not measured. Concrete mutation that survives: `kernels_may_run` (bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:350) returns `inflight` instead of `inflight || latched`. The latch state and `latched_flag` are still set, so `CHECK(unseen_latched())`, the unlatch loop and the final parks check all pass. `CHECK(median_last < 200)` is then the only check sensitive to the bug, and the expected value under the bug is about 195-200 us, so it is roughly a coin flip and depends on how quickly this machine wakes threads. The comment 'parked: about 500 us' is the figure for a random phase (c18) and does not apply to this kernel. As written, the test does not reliably verify what its name says: that unnoted requests keep the watcher from parking.
findings.fix: Check the effect of the latch directly. After the first unnoted kernel has latched the watcher, read `cuda_watcher_parks()`, run a second unnoted `calls(20, 2'000'000, false)` (requests keep the latch fresh), and require that the parks count did not advance, or advanced at most once. Alternatively, use a gap that does not line up with deferral plus parks, such as 2.5 ms (a parking watcher would answer in about 700 us), and lower the threshold to about 130 us. Fix the 'about 500 us' comment either way.

findings.title: Default-policy GPU tests do not pin BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE; with it exported they run WFE and the first one fails
findings.scenario: Only the WFE test scopes the variable (scoped_env "1"). `spaced_calls_fixture` creates its `bpf_attach_ctx` with whatever the environment holds, and the watcher reads `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE` when its thread starts. Example: a developer or measurement shell on the Orin has `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1` exported (it is the documented opt-in) and runs bpftime_runtime_tests. In 'answers spaced calls within a short sleep', the watcher then waits with WFE. `waiting_on_flag` stays true until the next event query, at most 1 ms after the kernel ends. `CHECK(!f.ctx->cuda_watcher_waits_on_flag())` runs about 50-100 us after `cuStreamSynchronize`, so it fails in most runs. The other two tests pass, but they test the WFE path instead of the default AC3 rules they are named for: latency ~15 us, and latched means WFE rather than 100 us sleeps.
findings.fix: Add a `scoped_env` member to `spaced_calls_fixture` that sets `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE` to "0" (or unsets it). Declare it before `ctx` so it is set before the watcher thread starts and restored after the ctx is destroyed.

findings.title: The watcher loop's use of the poll window and the 100 us sleeps is untested: disconnecting the window or polling instead of sleeping passes every test
findings.scenario: `[cuda-watcher-policy]` tests the `poll_window`, `deferral` and `unseen_launch_latch` classes on their own. The GPU tests use only 2 ms gaps, where the window is always 0, and check only upper bounds on latency. Mutation 1: `try_serve` never calls `window.on_request` (line 318), so the window never opens. The 2048-call burst in 'Every GPU thread's host call carries its own arguments' is then served by 20 us deferral sleeps, about 25-30 us per call. That is about 60 ms against `CHECK(elapsed < 200)` (line 801, about 20 ms expected), so the test still passes. All three new tests pass as well. The regression the window exists to prevent, 32-call bursts slowing to about 21-22 us per call (v3), goes unnoticed. Mutation 2: `sleep_us(w::slow_sleep_us)` (line 386) is replaced by `cpu_relax()`, so the watcher polls a whole core while a noted kernel runs. 'answers spaced calls within a short sleep' gets a lower median and passes, the parks test still sees parks while idle, and the latch test gets faster answers. No test checks that the watcher actually sleeps while a kernel runs, which is the CPU cost (0.1 core against 1 core) that AC3 was chosen for.
findings.fix: Add a GPU case for a short-gap burst with a tight bound. For example, 32 calls 10-20 us apart should take about 10 us per call with the window and 25+ us without it. Bound the burst test near its expected value (for example < 60 ms). Also count slow sleeps or poll iterations, like `cuda_watcher_parks`, and check them in the spaced-calls test: roughly one 100 us sleep per 100 us of kernel time, and no busy polling.

result.reasoning:
The mechanism described is accurate. The fault is not real: it is a test-hygiene suggestion, not a defect in the AC3 change.

What holds up:
- `cuda_watcher_can_wait_on_flag()` (`bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:208-218`) reads `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE` in the watcher thread when that thread starts.
- `spaced_calls_fixture` does not pin the variable.
- With WFE on, `waiting_on_flag` stays true after a kernel ends until the next `any_running()` query. That query runs at most every `event_query_every_us` = 1000 us (`cuda_watcher_policy.hpp:28`).
- So `CHECK(!f.ctx->cuda_watcher_waits_on_flag())` at `test_cuda_host_call.cpp:1430` would usually fail if WFE were on.

Why it does not count as a real defect:
1. In the default environment the tests are correct. WFE is now opt-in (`v == nullptr || strcmp(v, "1") != 0` returns false), and the three tests test exactly the default AC3 rules they are named for.
2. Nothing on this system sets the variable. It is not exported in `~/.zshrc`, `.zshenv`, `.zprofile`, `.profile`, `.bashrc` or `/etc/environment`. The measurement scripts pass their watcher settings per command (`EXP_ENV=(...)` in `watcher-policy-20261112/v{2,3}/scripts/run_one.sh`; `WFE_ENV=` inline in `wfe-load-20261111`), never as exports. The scenario needs a developer to export an opt-in tuning switch on purpose and then run the unit tests in that shell.
3. The suite never pins tuning variables in tests of default behavior. "Napping consumers are woken only when a buffer fills" does not pin `BPFTIME_CONSUMER_NAP_US` or `BPFTIME_CONSUMER_POLL_US`. The hash chain-collision test does not pin `BPFTIME_HASH_ZERO_SEED`. `grep` finds no setenv/unsetenv of those in `runtime/unit-test`. The only variables pinned are those a test sets itself (`BPFTIME_GLOBAL_SHM_NAME`, `BPFTIME_AOT_CACHE` in its own section). The tests here follow the same convention. The pre-change WFE test likewise did not guard against `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=0` being exported.
4. In that hypothetical case, a test of the default policy failing because the process was deliberately put in a non-default mode tells the developer the default is not in effect. The product and the tests behave correctly in the configuration they target.

Pinning the variable to "0" in the fixture would make the tests more robust, but that is an optional improvement, not a defect with a realistic failure scenario.

The finding is correct. Both mutations survive every test, and I found nothing that refutes them. It is only a gap in test coverage: the shipped code works correctly, and low severity fits.

Mutation 1: `window.on_request` is never called (bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:318).
- The window stays 0, so the polling branch never runs. Every call in a burst then waits for a 20 us deferral sleep. Each served request re-arms 8 of them, so the burst never reaches the park.
- The only GPU burst test is 'Every GPU thread's host call carries its own arguments': 2048 calls, `CHECK(elapsed < 200)` at line 801, about 20 ms expected. Its launch is unnoted (`test_module::launch` uses a null stream and never calls `note`).
- The measured data gives the cost. ACn (v3 README line 22: window off, WIN_MAX=0) costs 27.0 us per call in c06 (32 calls, no load), against 11.8 for AC3. That is about 55 ms for 2048 calls, well under the 200 ms bound, which allows about 98 us per call.
- The other GPU tests use only 2 ms gaps (lines 1425 and 1469) or single calls (line 1449). There every gap is at least 50 us, so the window stays 0 whether or not the mutation is applied.
- `[cuda-watcher-policy]` tests the `poll_window` class on its own, not how the loop uses it.

Mutation 2: `sleep_us(w::slow_sleep_us)` (line 386) becomes `cpu_relax()`.
- 'spaced calls within a short sleep' checks only `median < 150`, so busy polling gives a lower median and passes.
- The parks test runs while idle, and that path still parks.
- The latch test checks only `median_last < 200`, and the parks it counts after unlatching still happen.
- The capture test still passes, because event queries are rate-limited to every 1 ms inside `kernels_may_run`.
- The WFE test sets `BPFTIME_CUDA_WATCHER_WFE=1` and goes down the `wait_while_equal` path, so it never reaches the slow sleep.
- Nothing counts slow sleeps or measures the watcher's CPU time. I grepped the whole test file (1528 lines) and every file in dev.diff for `cuda_watcher`, `steady_clock`, `getrusage` and `/proc`.
- Yet CPU cost was why AC3 was chosen: in c23 M100 uses 1.039 cores against 0.104 for AC3.
- The test file itself cites mutation checks (line ~1332), so surviving mutations fall below the project's own bar.

Caveat on the proposed fix: a '< 60 ms' bound on the 2048-call test would not reliably separate the mutated cost (about 55 ms) from the limit. A 32-call short-gap case, and a slow-sleep or poll counter checked in the spaced-calls test, would catch these mutations.

The finding holds as a test-coverage defect, not a product bug. The latency figure is computed, not measured: it lands within a few microseconds of the threshold, on either side.

1. **The calls are phase-locked.** In `bpftime_test_spaced_calls` (test_cuda_host_call.cpp:369-425), `%rd6 = %globaltimer` is read at `$L_sc_next`, after the previous helper call has returned. Each 2 ms wait therefore starts when the watcher's last service returns.
   - The GPU-timed latency (`%rd13 - %rd11`) works out to (watcher cycle from one flag2 store to the next) - 2000 us - well under 1 us.
   - The GPU visibility and lock delays cancel out of it.

2. **What the mutant watcher does each cycle.** The mutant is `return inflight;` at bpf_attach_ctx_cuda.cpp:350.
   - The poll window stays 0: the first gap is UINT64_MAX and every later one is about 2.2 ms, so `long_gaps` reaches 2 and the window never opens.
   - The late-sleep guard never trips: `late_ewma` is about 0.
   - So after each request it takes 8 deferral sleeps, then parks repeatedly with the 1 ms backstop.
   - The c02 AC3 stats in v3 (same 1 us timer slack in both builds) give the durations:
     - Deferral sleeps: us_defer 612388 / 25608 = 23.9 us each.
     - Park timeouts: about 1004-1007 us each (us_park / parks, in all 4 rounds).
   - Park 1 ends near R+1196 us, before the request (about R+2005). Park 2 ends near R+2201 us.
   - Estimated latency: 8 x 23.9 + 2 x ~1005 + service - 2000, roughly 195-205 us on every call. That is right at `CHECK(median_last < 200)`, line 1476.
   - The real latched watcher sleeps 100 us at a time after the deferrals. It answers in roughly 0-110 us; M5.log shows a 61.9 us median, and the docs report 69-70 us. So the correct code passes easily.

3. **The mutant passes every other check.**
   - `latch.latched(t)` still runs inside `kernels_may_run`, so `latched_flag` is still stored.
   - Each park-2 end is a hit: generation unchanged, park lasted at least 1 ms, `flag1 == 1`. Two hits latch the watcher.
   - Each unnoted request keeps the latch fresh. So `CHECK(unseen_latched())` passes, the unlatch loop passes after 1 s, and the final check of at least 5 parks in 20 ms passes.

4. **No other test catches it.**
   - The other GPU tests either note their launches (lines 1279, 1312, 1398, 1517) or run dense bursts with no latency bound (the `module.launch()` tests).
   - `[cuda-watcher-policy]` tests only the latch class, not how the watcher loop uses it.
   - In /home/jetson/src/bpftime-gpu-work/ac3dev/mutate.py, M6 is the mirror mutation (`return latched;`). `return inflight;` was never run, so the project's rule that each mutation must make a test fail was not applied to it.

5. **The test comment is wrong for this kernel.** It says "parked: about 500 us". That figure fits a random phase: M7.log shows 427 us for a first call after idle, and c18 W shows 533 us. For this phase-locked kernel the expected value is about 200 us.
   - So the gap between the mutant's expected value and the threshold is a few microseconds.
   - That is smaller than the run-to-run drift seen in the latched median (61.9 vs 69-70 us), and it depends on how fast this machine wakes threads.
   - The check therefore cannot be relied on to show that unnoted requests keep the watcher from parking.

The suggested fixes would make the check sound: assert that `cuda_watcher_parks()` does not advance during a second unnoted run, or use a gap that is not phase-aligned.
